newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Deutsche Telekom says ready to go public.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Deutsche Telekom says ready to go public.

text.p: By William Boston German state-owned telecommunications giant, on Tuesday sought to dispel any doubts about its mammoth listing on international stock exchanges in November, saying it was ready to go public.

Just two months before it launches Europe's largest initial public offering ever, Telekom presented an interim report it hopes will convince analysts that it has completed its huge restructuring and is now set for steady growth.

"We have used the first half of this year to get in shape for our listing," Telekom chairman Ron Sommer told a news conference. "I believe that the numbers we have presented today provide a sound basis for calculations in the future."
Operating profits were set to more than double in 1996 from around four billion marks ($2.65 billion) the year before, Sommer added.
"Naturally our shareholders will benefit from this. We intend to propose paying dividends of around 1.5 billion marks," he said.
In an unusual move to attract investors, the company said it would announce next month how big a dividend it would pay on 1997 results.
"In the first year after our listing, we will be able to pay a dividend that will rank among the highest in Germany," said Telekom finance chief Joachim Kroeske.

Earnings in the first half of 1996 were marked by huge restructuring costs to pay for job cuts to the year 2000, the first-time payment of sales tax, and a 500 million mark dent in sales in January after a confusing revamp of phone charges.

According to data adjusted to comparable results had it paid taxes in 1995, pre-tax profit was 2.7 billion marks in the first half of 1996, up 22.7 percent. Sales slipped 1.4 percent to 29.7 billion marks. Net income, hit by restructuring charges of 1.85 billion marks, plunged 82 percent to 129 million marks.
Calculated according to U.S. Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP), Telekom's net earnings were 521 million marks in the first half. It gave no comparison.

Not adjusted for the effects of sales tax, Telekom pre-tax profit slid 50.1 percent to 2.7 billion marks in the first half from 5.4 billion. Net income plunged 96.3 percent to 129 million marks. Sales fell 5.9 percent to 30.6 billion marks.
Analysts close to Telekom's preparations for its listing warned against reading too much into the net income fall.
"It's not very meaningful to compare at the net level," one analyst said on condition of anonymity.
According to his analysis of Telekom's data, pre-tax profit rose 51.6 percent on an adjusted basis to 3.32 billion marks.

On an EBITDA basis (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation), which is widely used by U.S. analysts, Telekom earnings were 7.2 billion marks in the first half, up 13.2 percent from the previous year, he said.
Telekom will list shares on stock exchanges in Germany, New York and possibly Tokyo and Canada beginning November 18.
New shares will result from a capital increase that the government will decline to subscribe to, making it possible for to raise up to 15 billion marks in capital on stock markets.

The government's stake in Telekom will fall to around 80 percent and fall again to around two-thirds when a second batch of shares are sold in 1998. The government is not allowed to sell its remaining shares until after the year 2000.

Despite the difficulties interpreting Telekom's earnings, there is clear evidence it is making progress. Telekom's debt at the end of June was 105.5 billion marks, down 20 billion marks since it was incorporated at the beginning of 1995.
The company added 1.75 billion marks to reserves to cover its planned staff reduction to 170,000 in the year 2000.
No further restructuring charges are expected for the next four years. Pension payments for civil servants, around 55 percent of the workforce, will fall sharply after 2000.
Staff levels fell by 14,000 to 207,000 employees at the end of June. Personnel costs fell 0.8 percent to 9.4 billion marks.
